questions.q: In what year did Constantine I officially dedicate Constantinople as the new capital of the Roman Empire, and what was the city's earlier name?
questions.a: Constantine dedicated Constantinople in 324 CE (formally inaugurated 330 CE); the city was formerly the Greek colony of Byzantium. A wrong answer (e.g., 312 CE, the Battle of Milvian Bridge, or "Rome") reveals confusion between Constantine's conversion, his victory over Licinius, and the actual foundation of the eastern capital — a common chronology error in board exams.

questions.q: Why did the eastern Roman Empire survive the 5th-century Germanic invasions that destroyed the western empire, despite facing similar pressures?
questions.a: The east survived because: (1) its capital Constantinople was defensible by sea and land with massive walls; (2) it retained richer, more urbanised provinces (Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor) generating stable tax revenue in gold; (3) it maintained a professional field army paid in solidi, not foederati; (4) emperors like Zeno and Anastasius used diplomacy (subsidies, marriage alliances) to divert invaders westward. A wrong answer focusing only on "stronger walls" or "better emperors" misses the systemic fiscal-military-diplomatic integration that Class 11 requires.

questions.q: Analyse the following statement using evidence from the 6th century: "Justinian's reconquest of the western Mediterranean strengthened the Byzantine Empire in the long run." Support or refute with three specific consequences.
questions.a: Refute. Consequences: (1) Fiscal exhaustion — the Gothic War (535–554) devastated Italy's economy and cost ~300,000 lbs of gold, emptying Anastasius's treasury surplus; (2) Overextension — garrisons in Africa, Italy, Spain stretched the army thin, leaving the Balkan and eastern frontiers undermanned against Slavs and Persians; (3) Plague vulnerability — the 541–549 bubonic plague spread rapidly along reconquest supply lines, killing ~25–50% of the population. A "support" answer ignores the structural trade-off between territorial ambition and core resilience — a key analytical skill for "evaluate" questions.

questions.q: Compare the administrative response of the eastern empire to the 7th-century crisis (Heraclius, 610–641) with Diocletian's 3rd-century reforms. Identify two structural similarities and one critical difference in military organisation.
questions.a: Similarities: (1) Both separated civilian and military authority to prevent usurpation; (2) Both reorganised provinces into smaller units for tighter control. Difference: Diocletian created mobile comitatenses and limitanei under central command; Heraclius created the theme system where soldier-farmers (stratiotai) held land grants (stratiotika ktemata) in exchange for hereditary military service, decentralising defence and reducing cash salary dependence. A wrong answer conflating "theme" with "province" or missing the land-for-service swap shows lack of grasp on the evolution from late Roman to medieval Byzantine military-fiscal structure.

questions.q: Evaluate the historian A.H.M. Jones's claim that "the Byzantine Empire was the Roman Empire in its medieval phase." Use evidence from religion, law, language, and army to justify your position.
questions.a: Partially valid but requires nuance. Continuity: Roman law (Corpus Juris Civilis, 529–534), imperial ideology (basileus as God's vice-regent), bureaucracy, and citizenship concept persisted. Transformation: Greek replaced Latin as administrative language (7th century); Orthodox Christianity became state ideology with caesaropapism; theme army replaced professional legions; economy shifted from monetary to semi-naturalised. The empire was Roman in legal-political DNA but Byzantine in socio-cultural expression. A binary "yes/no" answer fails the "evaluate" demand for weighed judgement with multi-dimensional evidence.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (324–642 CE) showing the causal chain from Constantine's foundation to the Arab conquests, with annotations explaining how each event altered the empire's fiscal-military capacity. Include at least 8 dated events.
questions.a: Sample timeline: 324 – Constantinople founded (strategic capital, tax hub); 395 – Final east-west split (separate fiscal systems); 491–518 – Anastasius's reforms (abolished chrysargyron, built 320,000 lbs gold reserve); 527–565 – Justinian's reign (reconquest costs, plague, legal codification); 541–549 – Plague of Justinian (demographic-fiscal shock); 602–628 – Byzantine-Sasanian War (exhausted both empires); 610–641 – Heraclius (theme system inception, True Cross recovery); 633–642 – Arab conquests (loss of Egypt/Syria = 60% revenue, 50% manpower). Each annotation must link event to fiscal-military capacity change. Poor answers list events without causal annotation.
